spec.cue: The view is a wide ring of soft light. Ultraviolet, blue and green are shown in false colour, and the picture runs a little slower than yours, then jumps ahead.

cpd.note: highest detail a honeybee worker resolves

fov.note: whole-animal horizontal field, a general bee figure

fovea.note: no sharp middle is drawn beyond the zone below

rate.note: slows the picture so that a bee's faster flicker sight can be felt

living.note: no extra weight for living movement

sat.note: keeps colour as a person sees it, apart from the false colour map

BEE.note: ultraviolet shown as blue, blue as green, green as red; red dropped, following the false colour convention in the lunau review

field.name: squeeze

colour.name: palm

rows: A honeybee resolves detail only as fine as about a quarter of a grating cycle per degree, roughly one two-hundredth of what a person sees. Its middle is no sharper than its edge, so the picture stays soft all over.
A bee sees close to the whole way round, with a small blind region behind and below. The view is squeezed to fit a wide field.

Bees have three kinds of colour receptor, in ultraviolet, blue and green, so they see ultraviolet which people cannot. This view shows ultraviolet as blue, blue as green and green as red, and drops red, because bees do not see far red.
A bee sees flicker faster than people do, up to about 200 times a second in bright light. Its picture is reported to be faster than ours, so this view moves more slowly to suggest the difference.
A bee turns its head in quick jumps of 5 to 60 degrees, then holds its view still between jumps.
The glow, its colour, the gain, the speed of the picture, the wide soft ring and the false colour grid are the app's own choices to make the bee's view easy to picture. No record gives these numbers.

claims.how: The honeybee worker's highest resolved frequency is recorded as 0.26 cycles per degree.
The general bee field of view is given as about 300 degrees horizontally, a general figure rather than a measured one for this species.
The middle zone uses the same measured sharpness as the whole picture.

quotes.quote: They found that the highest spatial frequency reliably resolved by the bees was 0.26 cycle deg−1, with no evidence of a difference in acuity between horizontal and vertical gratings.
Bees can see ~300° horizontally on the body plane with low spatial resolution for peripheral ommatidia
At ca. 200 Hz the FRC drops to 50%.
The temporal resolution of colour vision, determined to be at 100 Hz in free-flying bees through measurements of the flicker-fusion frequency
‘saccades’, when angular velocities of the head reach up to 1500°/sec (see Fig 2C), and ‘intersaccades’, when the yaw orientation of the head is kept virtually constant.
In contrast to us, bees can see UV light but not far red.
using a (bathochromic) shift to longer wavelengths, by which UV is shown as blue, blue as green, green as red and red is discarded
collects a composite image of the panorama in radial coordinates over about 200° horizontally
Seidl and Kaiser (1981) reported that the honeybee FOV extends down to −90° in elevation and back to −156° in azimuth (at 0° el.)
The orientation of the gratings can be clearly observed even with 2° patterns and the imaged gratings are quite sharp.
